Where each figure comes from

  • GSUA General Staff of Ukraine's Armed Forces — casualties, equipment, combat activity, air attacks, strike counts and key targets hit
  • KIU Killed-in-Ukraine — confirmed named losses, including officers
  • Lussier Simon-Pierre Lussier — Russian officers killed, by date of death
  • Mediazona Mediazona — Russian deaths confirmed by name, including officers
  • UALosses UALosses — Ukrainian soldiers killed, missing or captured, confirmed by name
  • Oryx Jakub Janovsky / Oryx — visually confirmed equipment
  • Valka Valka.online — visually confirmed equipment losses per month; months Valka has not published yet are preliminary, calculated from the change in Oryx's lists over the month
  • Estimates NATO, CSIS, British intelligence and Mediazona / Meduza — estimates of Russian deaths
  • Zelenskyy Volodymyr Zelenskyy, via Politico — the share of deaths among casualties (26.47%) behind the estimated Russian deaths
  • Air Force Air Force of Ukraine — overnight drone and missile attacks, and how many were shot down
  • DroneBomber DroneBomber — Ukrainian strike drones over Russia, citing Russian sources
  • Russian MoD Russian Ministry of Defence — its claims of Ukrainian drones shot down
  • Ukrenergo Ukrenergo — power cuts after Russian strikes on the grid, and scheduled outages
  • ISW Institute for the Study of War — territorial control
  • DeepState DeepStateMap — territorial control and the occupied area on the maps
  • Russia Matters Russia Matters War Report Card — area gained, citing DeepState, ISW and The Economist
  • GeoNames GeoNames — locations of the places on the maps
  • Open-Meteo weather at the front, retrieved by script

Civilians and beyond the battlefield

  • UN HRMMU UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine — civilian casualties, and the Russian authorities' figures it quotes
  • Children of War Children of War portal — deported, returned, killed, injured and missing children
  • Coordination HQ Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War — prisoner exchanges
  • Eurostat Eurostat — temporary protection in the EU
  • UNHCR / IOM UNHCR and IOM — refugees worldwide and internally displaced people
  • CREA CREA Russia Fossil Tracker — Russia's fossil fuel export revenue
  • Minfin Russian Ministry of Finance — oil and gas budget revenue
  • Kiel Kiel Institute Ukraine Support Tracker — aid to Ukraine
  • World Bank World Bank — GDP (PPP) for aid as a share of GDP

Reading the marks

▲ >2% better for Ukraine
~ ±2% broadly unchanged
▼ <-2% worse for Ukraine
★ Record highest day ever
Top 10 · #9 historically notable
Gold never means good or bad — it marks a figure that is unusual by its own history. On Russian strike counts the green/red scale inverts: fewer strikes is the good outcome.

Guide to the figures

Record — top-10 days

Every daily figure is ranked against every other day of the war for that same category. A tank figure is only ever compared with other tank figures, so a small absolute number can still be historically high.

★ Record
The highest single day ever recorded for that category, or a match of it.
Top 10
Among the ten highest days of the war for that category.
#38
Inside the top fifty — worth noticing, but not remarkable.
#412
An ordinary day by that category's standards.

The Record column only shows a badge when the latest day is among the ten highest of the whole war, or among the ten highest of the current year (outlined badge). Gold never carries direction. Green and red carry direction only.

Key targets hit

The headlines of the General Staff's “Уражено …” (“Hit: …”) posts about Ukrainian strikes, mostly deep strikes inside Russia and occupied territory, translated to English and sorted into categories such as oil and fuel, defence industry, radars or drone sites. The date is the day of the post; the strikes themselves are usually from the night before. A headline can name several targets, so it can carry several categories. Click the box for the list of recent days, filter by category, and follow each item to the original post.

Where the data comes from

A filled badge — GSUA — marks figures reported by the General Staff of Ukraine's Armed Forces. These are Ukrainian claims and are not independently verified. A dashed badge — Oryx — marks a third party, and those cards carry a dashed border. Third-party counts are slower and far more conservative, which is why the two are never mixed in one figure.

What the columns mean

Latest day
The most recent daily figure, covering the activity date in the ribbon above.
vs day before
Absolute change against the preceding daily figure.
7-day avg
Mean of the seven most recent daily figures.
Latest vs avg
How far the most recent day sits above or below that average.
Last 7 days
Sum of the seven most recent daily figures.
vs previous 7
Percentage change against the seven days before those.
Daily record
The highest single-day figure ever recorded for that item.
Since invasion
Cumulative total reported since 24 February 2022.

Timestamps

The report date is when this page was compiled. The activity date is the day the General Staff figures cover. The time shown beside the weather is when the weather itself was retrieved from Open-Meteo by script — it says nothing about when the casualty figures were published.

Caveats

Casualties count killed and wounded together; the estimated-deaths line applies a fixed share derived from released data. Equipment figures are field reports, which run well ahead of the visually confirmed counts — both are shown so the gap stays visible.

Where the page gets its data

Three transports, tried in the order listed in CONFIG.sources. The first that answers wins, and the snapshot baked into this file is the last resort, so the page never renders empty.

data.json
A static file published beside this page every morning. It is built from the spreadsheets by the Ukraine dashboard auto-update Apps Script. The spreadsheets stay entirely private — their IDs never appear here. Recommended.
Published CSV
Sheets → File → Share → Publish to web, one tab at a time, format CSV. Only the tabs you tick become public and the document stays unshared. Paste each URL into CONFIG.csv.
gviz
The legacy path. It needs the whole document shared as “anyone with the link”, which exposes every tab in it, not just the five the page reads. Leave spreadsheetId empty to disable.

The shape of the data

Column order never matters — headers are matched by name, case and punctuation ignored.

meta       key | value
           keys: reportdate, activitydate, activityiso,
                 weatherupdated, areaasof, weather (JSON)
headline   id | label | value | unit | dec | exact | delta | deltaUnit
           | deltaLabel | invert | note | source | lead | goodNote
metrics    id | group | label | sublabel | value | unit | dec
           | delta | deltaUnit | deltaLabel | invert | plain
equipment  id | label | sublabel | record | recordNote | rank
           | total | day | chgDay | last7 | chg7 | avg7 | vsAvg | aggregate
series     date | troops | equipment | <item id> ...
           one extra column per equipment id (uav, tank, arty …)
           feeds the category picker on the equipment chart

rank is the position of that day's figure among all daily figures for that category, 1 being the all-time high. Leave it blank and the badge falls back to the record comparison. source takes gsua or a third-party name such as ISW.

A data.json file carries the same information already assembled, plus a generated timestamp that the status line shows. Anything it leaves out keeps the snapshot's value, so a partial file is safe to publish.

How the places were found
  • Each “Уражено” post is read in full, and every target is placed at the settlement, facility or region the post names. Dates are when the post appeared; the strikes are usually from the night before. These are Ukrainian claims, not independently verified.
  • Located: the settlement was found in the GeoNames gazetteer inside the region the post names.
  • Approximate (dashed ring): a town, refinery or airfield placed from general knowledge, or a small village that is not in the gazetteer or shares its name with others nearby. These can be off by several kilometres, small villages by more.
  • Ships at sea and targets with no place named are listed but not drawn. Occupied area: DeepStateMap, .

Locations are approximate. Places are matched by name from the General Staff reports, so a village that shares its name with another can end up in the wrong spot, and dashed rings can be several kilometres off.

How the map is made
  • Each morning General Staff report (08:00 Kyiv) is read in full. Every place it names is put on the map with its front direction and the kind of activity. Dates are the day of the fighting, the day before the report.
  • Attack counts per direction are the numbers stated in the reports. Air strikes and shelling are mostly the Sumy and Chernihiv border areas, which the reports list separately.
  • Located places were matched to the GeoNames gazetteer near the expected spot on that direction. Approximate places (dashed ring) were placed from general knowledge, usually because several villages share the name, and can be off by several kilometres.
  • Occupied area: DeepStateMap, .
